course_information.title: Surface Preparation & Painting Tools
course_information.description: Identify common preparation steps and application tools so customers can prepare and paint more effectively.
course_information.scope: General independent hardware retail; not store-specific

Identify common repair, sanding, masking, and protection supplies.

Use label directions to explain preparation and cleanup.
Recognize hazardous or complex situations requiring escalation.

lessons.title: Start with a Clean, Sound Surface
lessons.objective: Explain why preparation comes before painting.
lessons.why_this_matters: Even a good coating can fail when the surface is dirty, loose, or wet.

content.heading: Inspect before coating
content.text: Look for dust, grease, loose paint, damaged areas, and moisture. The customer should identify and correct underlying problems before painting.

content.heading: Clean as directed
content.text: Cleaning methods vary by surface and coating. Use manufacturer instructions and allow required drying time.

content.heading: Do not paint over a problem
content.text: Paint is not a fix for leaks, structural damage, or active mold. Old coatings may need special precautions.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants to paint over peeling paint on a damp wall. You recommend investigating the moisture cause before buying a new topcoat.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “Is the wall dry now, and do you know why the paint is peeling?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming primer solves moisture; coating over loose material.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate suspected lead paint, mold, persistent dampness, and structural damage. Do not advise disturbing unknown older coatings.

lessons.title: Understand Patching and Sanding
lessons.objective: Recognize basic repair supplies and when they are appropriate.
lessons.why_this_matters: Small defects may need repair before the final finish is applied.

content.heading: Match repair material to damage
content.text: Spackling products, fillers, and patch materials have different intended uses. Confirm the surface, depth, and manufacturer directions.

content.heading: Sanding has a purpose
content.text: Sanding can smooth a repair or prepare a surface when the coating instructions call for it. Grit numbers indicate abrasive coarseness; lower numbers are generally coarser.

content.heading: Control dust and exposure
content.text: Follow product safety instructions. Do not recommend sanding suspected lead-containing paint or unknown hazardous coatings.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer has a small nail hole in painted drywall. You help them locate a patching product labeled for small interior wall repairs and the recommended finishing supplies.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “How large is the hole, and is the surface drywall, wood, or something else?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Using wood filler for every wall repair; recommending sanding without checking hazards.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask for help with large cracks, water damage, structural issues, or suspected lead coatings.

lessons.title: Mask and Protect the Work Area
lessons.objective: Identify tools that protect nearby surfaces and control paint placement.
lessons.why_this_matters: Preparation saves cleanup time and protects the customer’s belongings.

content.heading: Cover what should not be painted
content.text: Drop cloths and protective coverings help protect floors, furniture, and fixtures. Select materials suitable for the location.

content.heading: Use tape correctly
content.text: Painter’s tapes differ in surface compatibility and removal timing. Check the package instructions; some delicate surfaces need special care.

content.heading: Plan safe access
content.text: Use appropriate access equipment and follow its instructions. Do not suggest unsafe ladder setups or work near electrical hazards.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer plans to paint trim beside a finished wood floor. You discuss floor protection and tape labeled for the adjoining surfaces.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “What surfaces need protection, and are any freshly painted or delicate?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Using any tape on any surface; forgetting floor protection.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate high work areas, damaged ladders, or work around exposed wiring.

lessons.title: Select Brushes and Rollers
lessons.objective: Match application tools to the surface and coating.
lessons.why_this_matters: The right tool makes application easier and can improve consistency.

content.heading: Brushes for control
content.text: Brushes are useful for edges, trim, and smaller areas. Bristle material and shape should match the coating and task per product guidance.

content.heading: Rollers for broad areas
content.text: Roller cover nap, material, and width affect application. Textured surfaces may need a different cover than smooth walls.

content.heading: Accessories matter
content.text: Trays, grids, extension poles, and compatible applicators support the job. Always check the coating label for recommended tools.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer is painting a smooth interior wall and rough masonry. You explain why the same roller cover may not be ideal for both.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Is the surface smooth or textured? Let’s check the paint’s recommended applicator.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming one roller works everywhere; choosing only by price.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a specialist about specialty coatings, spraying, or incompatible applicator materials.

lessons.title: Plan Application and Cleanup
lessons.objective: Explain why timing, ventilation, and cleanup instructions matter.
lessons.why_this_matters: The project continues after the first coat is applied.

content.heading: Follow application conditions
content.text: Product directions may set temperature, humidity, ventilation, and recoating requirements. Check them rather than using a universal rule.

content.heading: Separate recoat from full use
content.text: A surface may be ready for another coat before it is ready for cleaning or heavy use.

content.heading: Clean up by product instructions
content.text: Water-based and solvent-based products can require different cleanup and disposal practices. Follow the label and local disposal rules; never advise pouring leftover coatings or solvents into drains.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks whether they can wash a newly painted wall tomorrow. You check the specific paint’s return-to-service and cleaning guidance.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s read this product’s instructions for recoating, cleaning, and disposal.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Guessing dry times; suggesting disposal down a sink; ignoring ventilation.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate solvent hazards, spray applications, disposal uncertainty, or symptoms from exposure.
